topics.name: Depreciation: methods and rules
topics.why: Thursday's test. Learn the two methods and the policy wording, then drill the numbers.
topics.notes:
Depreciation is an estimate of the fall in value of a non-current asset (machines, motor vehicles, buildings). Causes: wear and tear, usage, time, technology (obsolescence).

This year's charge goes to the P&L as an expense. The running total sits in the SOFP under non-current assets as accumulated depreciation: Cost − Acc dep = NBV.

Straight line (SL): Cost × rate (same every year) Reducing balance (RB): (Cost − Acc dep) × rate (= NBV × rate, falls every year)

Read the policy line first. Mags uses two:

  • "Full year in the year of purchase, none in the year of sale": every past paper uses this one. Count financial years, not months.
  • "One month's ownership means one month's depreciation" (Q25.1A, Q25.2A): charge × months owned ÷ 12.
Trap: with RB, the charge is on the NBV of the assets still held at year end: (closing cost − acc dep of the assets you still have) × rate. Take the sold asset's acc dep out first.

topics.name: Ledger accounts and disposals
topics.why: This is where the marks are: cost, acc dep and disposal accounts. Follow the 7 steps until they're automatic.
topics.notes:
Mags's 7 steps (from the depreciation solutions file). Follow them in this order every time:

  1. Enter the opening balances in the Cost a/c (Dr) and Acc Dep a/c (Cr).
  2. Enter purchases for the year in the Cost a/c (Dr bank).
  3. For a disposal: Cr Cost a/c with the asset's cost (Dr Disposal), and Dr Acc Dep a/c with its accumulated depreciation (Cr Disposal).
  4. Balance the Cost account. This gives the closing cost.
  5. Calculate this year's depreciation (Cr Acc Dep, Dr P&L).
  6. Finish the Disposal account: Cr proceeds or trade-in. The balancing figure is profit (Dr side) or loss (Cr side).
  7. Balance the Acc Dep account.
Disposal a/c Dr Cost of asset sold Cr Acc dep on asset sold Dr Profit on disposal (→ P&L income) Cr Proceeds / trade-in allowance Cr Loss on disposal (→ P&L expense)

Trade-in: proceeds = trade-in allowance = new asset's cost − cash paid. The new asset still goes into the Cost a/c at its full cost: Dr Cost (full price), Cr Bank (cash paid), Cr Disposal (allowance).

Over-depreciated (NBV < proceeds) → profit on disposal. Under-depreciated (NBV > proceeds) → loss.

topics.name: P&L and SOFP (Section A, 40 marks)
topics.why: Compulsory in December. Learn the layout and practise building it from a trial balance.
topics.notes:
Section A, compulsory, 40 marks: P&L (25) and SOFP (15) from a trial balance, with two adjustments: closing inventory and depreciation.

Sales − Sales returns = Net sales Opening inv + Purchases − Purchases returns + Carriage inwards − Closing inv = Cost of sales Net sales − Cost of sales = Gross profit + Discount received (and other income) − Expenses (incl. depreciation, carriage outwards, discount allowed, loan interest) = Net profit / (loss)

topics.name: Double entry
topics.why: Fast debit/credit decisions. Flashcards and quick questions until you don't hesitate.
topics.notes:
Every transaction has a debit and an equal credit. Debit the account that receives value, credit the account that gives value.

DEBIT increases: Assets · Expenses · Drawings CREDIT increases: Capital · Liabilities · Income (sales, purchases returns, discount received)
TransactionDebitCredit
Owner lodges savingsBankCapital
Machine bought on credit from Wing LtdMachineryWing Ltd (payable)
Goods bought on credit from Foley LtdPurchasesFoley Ltd
Goods sold on credit to Shiny LtdShiny Ltd (receivable)Sales
We return goods to FoleyFoley LtdPurchases returns
Shiny returns goods to usSales returnsShiny Ltd
Paid wages by chequeWagesBank
Owner takes cash / stock for private useDrawingsBank / Purchases
Received cheque from ShinyBankShiny Ltd
Insurance €1,500, 40% privateInsurance 900 + Drawings 600Bank 1,500
Trap: "in full settlement" for less than the balance means the difference is a discount. Paying a payable less: Cr Discount received. A receivable paying us less: Dr Discount allowed.

Balance each account: the bigger side's total goes on both sides, and the gap is bal c/d, carried to the opposite side as bal b/d.

topics.name: Day books and VAT
topics.why: Mechanical: net, VAT at 23%, total, then post the totals. Accuracy beats speed.
topics.notes:
Credit transactions with VAT (23%) are listed first in day books, then the totals are posted to the nominal ledger.

Day bookPosting of totals
Sales day book (Net · VAT · Total)Dr Receivables control (total) · Cr Sales (net) · Cr VAT (VAT)
Purchases day bookDr Purchases (net) · Dr VAT (VAT) · Cr Payables control (total)
Sales returns day bookDr Sales returns (net) · Dr VAT · Cr Receivables control
Purchases returns day bookDr Payables control · Cr Purchases returns (net) · Cr VAT
Cash receipts bookDr Bank · Cr Receivables control
Cheque payments bookDr Payables control · Cr Bank
Net = units × price VAT = Net × 23% Total = Net + VAT e.g. 987 × €4.89 = €4,826.43 → VAT €1,110.08 → Total €5,936.51

VAT a/c: VAT on sales and purchases returns on the Cr side (owed to Revenue), VAT on purchases and sales returns on the Dr side. A credit balance is a current liability.

Part C (6 marks): why users care about the accounts. Bank: can they repay the loan and interest, is there security, would they qualify for a future loan. Employee: job security, wages paid, future prospects. Revenue: correct income tax, VAT, PAYE/PRSI/USC paid.

topics.name: Users of accounts and expenditure
topics.why: Easy marks in Part C questions. Memorise who wants what.
topics.notes:
Qualities of financial information: accurate and timely, clear and concise, relevant, comparable.

UserWhat they want to know
Owner (sole trader)Is it profitable, liquid, and what's its future potential
InvestorsIs it a good investment, share price, retained earnings for dividends
Revenue CommissionersAll taxes paid: VAT, PAYE/PRSI/USC, income tax, corporation tax
Banks and lendersLoan repayments and interest can be paid, security on the loan
Payables (suppliers)Will they be paid on time
CustomersGuarantee on products, future after-care service
EmployeesWages paid, job security, future prospects and promotion
CompetitorsHow they compare, and whether they can take market share
Management and directorsIs the business thriving, liquid and competitive

Revenue expenditure: day-to-day running costs (stock, wages, electricity, insurance). All of it goes to the P&L in the year it occurs.

Capital expenditure: benefits the business for more than a year (equipment, buildings, vehicles). It's capitalised in the SOFP and sent to the P&L gradually through depreciation, e.g. a €100,000 machine with a 5-year life sends €20,000 a year.

questions.q: Depreciation is best described as:
o: The cash set aside to replace an asset
An estimate of the fall in value of a non-current asset
The market value of an asset
questions.e: It's an estimate. You only find out how accurate it was when you sell the asset.

questions.q: Which is NOT a cause of depreciation?
questions.e: Mags's list: wear and tear, usage, time, technology.

questions.q: A machine costs €40,000. Depreciation is 15% straight line. The annual charge is:
questions.e: SL: cost × rate = 40,000 × 15% = €6,000 every year.

questions.e: It's a % of a shrinking NBV.

questions.e: Expense in the P&L (Dr), built up in the accumulated depreciation account (Cr).

o: Opening inv + purchases − purchases returns + carriage in − closing inv
questions.e: Carriage inwards is part of cost of sales. Carriage outwards is an expense.

questions.q: Carriage outwards is shown as:

cards.b: Cost × rate. The same charge every year.
(Cost − acc dep) × rate = NBV × rate. Falls every year.
Wear and tear, usage, time, technology (obsolescence).

cards.f: Where does this year's depreciation go?
cards.b: Dr P&L (expense), Cr accumulated depreciation account.
SOFP, non-current assets: Cost − Acc dep = NBV.

cards.f: 'Full year in year of purchase, none in year of sale'
cards.b: Count financial years held, ignoring months. Bought Y/E 2021, sold Y/E 2026 → 5 years.
Annual charge × months owned ÷ 12. Bought 1 July with Dec year end → 6/12.
1 Opening balances · 2 Purchases into cost · 3 Disposal: cost out (Cr), its acc dep out (Dr) · 4 Balance cost a/c · 5 This year's dep · 6 Disposal a/c · 7 Balance acc dep a/c.
Cost of the asset sold (+ profit on disposal as the balancing figure).
Acc dep on the asset sold + proceeds or trade-in (+ loss as the balancing figure).
Over-depreciated: NBV < proceeds. Goes to the P&L as income.
Under-depreciated: NBV > proceeds. Goes to the P&L as an expense.
New asset cost − cash paid. Credit it to the disposal account as proceeds.

cards.f: Trade-in: new asset in cost account at…
cards.b: Its FULL cost. Cr Bank (cash) and Cr Disposal (allowance).

cards.b: (Closing cost − acc dep of assets still held) × rate. Take the sold asset's acc dep out first.

cards.f: SL charge when there's been a disposal
cards.b: Closing cost × rate (the cost account balance after additions and disposals).
Opening inv + purchases − purchases returns + carriage inwards − closing inv.
(Sales − sales returns) − cost of sales.
Closing inventory (cost of sales AND current asset) and depreciation (P&L expense AND SOFP acc dep).
Inwards → cost of sales. Outwards → expense.
Opening capital + net profit (or − loss) − drawings.

cards.f: Credit bank balance in the TB
cards.b: Overdraft → current liability.
Payables, VAT (Cr), PAYE/PRSI, bank overdraft.
Debit the account that RECEIVES value. Assets, expenses and drawings increase on the debit side.
Credit the account that GIVES value. Capital, liabilities and income increase on the credit side.

Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases.

Difference = discount allowed (Dr, expense).
Dr Receivables control (total) · Cr Sales (net) · Cr VAT.
Dr Purchases (net) · Dr VAT · Cr Payables control (total).
Owed to Revenue → current liability.

Financial Accounting Principles · Assignment 2 (15%) · Thursday 19 November, 1pm

1. Read the policy line first

  • Full year in year of purchase, none in year of sale: count financial years held.
  • One month's ownership = one month's depreciation: × months ÷ 12.

2. Formulas

SL charge = Closing cost × rate RB charge = (Closing cost − acc dep of assets STILL HELD) × rate NBV = Cost − Acc dep Trade-in allowance = New asset cost − cash paid Profit/(loss) on disposal = Proceeds − NBV

3. The 7 steps

  1. Opening balances: Cost a/c (Dr), Acc dep a/c (Cr)
  2. Purchases → Dr Cost a/c (Cr Bank). Trade-in: full cost, split Cr Bank / Cr Disposal
  3. Disposal: Cr Cost a/c with its cost → Dr Disposal · Dr Acc dep with its acc dep → Cr Disposal
  4. Balance the Cost account
  5. This year's charge: Dr P&L, Cr Acc dep
  6. Disposal a/c: Cr proceeds / trade-in → balancing figure = profit (Dr side) or loss (Cr side)
  7. Balance the Acc dep account

4. RB: acc dep on a disposed asset

Yr 1: Cost × r = D1 NBV1 = Cost − D1 Yr 2: NBV1 × r = D2 NBV2 = NBV1 − D2 Acc dep on disposal = D1 + D2 + … (years held, none in year of sale)

5. Account layouts

Cost a/c — DrCr
Bal b/d · Bank (additions) · Disposal (trade-in part)Disposal (cost of asset sold) · Bal c/d
Acc dep a/c — DrCr
Disposal (acc dep of asset sold) · Bal c/dBal b/d · P&L (this year's charge)
Disposal a/c — DrCr
Cost a/c (cost) · P&L (profit)Acc dep · Bank / trade-in · P&L (loss)

6. Checks before you hand up

  • Dates on every entry, with "bal b/d" on the first day of each year
  • Both years done if asked for two years
  • RB: did you take the sold asset's acc dep out BEFORE calculating the charge?
  • Profit means over-depreciated, loss means under-depreciated
  • SOFP extract if asked: Cost | Acc dep | NBV
